subject_area: Algorithm analysis and design — classical CS theory
course_intent: Teach students how to design, analyze, and reason about the correctness and asymptotic efficiency of classical algorithms — students should leave able to apply standard algorithmic paradigms (divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, greedy), analyze running time using recurrences and asymptotic notation, and understand foundational data-structure and graph algorithms.
depth_bound: Recommendations stay at the level of classical algorithmic paradigms, asymptotic analysis, and pseudocode-level algorithm design. Implementation tutorials in specific languages, advanced topics like randomized/approximation algorithms, parallel/distributed algorithms, and competitive-programming-style problem sets are beyond this course's depth bound.
key_topics: Asymptotic notation (Θ, O, Ω, o, ω) and growth-rate analysis
Recurrence-solving methods (iteration, substitution, recursion tree, master theorem)
Divide-and-conquer (merge sort, binary search, Strassen's matrix multiplication)
Dynamic programming (rod cutting, longest common subsequence, memoization vs tabulation)
Elementary graph representations (adjacency list vs matrix) and graph traversal
Correctness proofs via loop invariants and mathematical induction
Comparison-based sorting algorithms and their analysis
one_liner: Classical undergraduate algorithms course covering asymptotic analysis, recurrences, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, balanced BSTs, and elementary graph algorithms at the pseudocode/analysis level — does NOT cover language-specific implementation, randomized/approximation algorithms, or advanced topics like network flow, NP-completeness depth, or parallel algorithms.
